scope_reminder: No playtime/engagement data exists anywhere in this dataset (all playtime columns constant zero). owners_mid is a linear midpoint of a SteamSpy bucketed range, not a measured count -- 83.2% of the catalogue sits in the single bottom bucket (0..20,000), so owners_mid has near-zero resolution below ~20k and all owners-based statistics below are dominated by the upper tail, not typical titles. All findings are Steam PC catalogue evidence; Stage 3's context establishes console ARPPU ~48% higher than PC and a genre-mix gap (PC skews shooter, Xbox console skews sports) -- direct transfer of any Steam-only finding to the Xbox console population is a stated limitation, not an assumption.

findings.claim: Estimated audience is extremely hit-concentrated across every major gaming genre: the top 10% of titles by owners_mid capture 78-93% of the genre's total estimated audience, while 75-86% of titles sit in SteamSpy's lowest resolution bucket (under ~20,000 owners).
findings.uncertainty: owners_mid is a coarse bucket-midpoint proxy; the top-decile-share figure is directionally robust across genres despite the proxy's coarseness because it compares titles within the same measurement error, but exact percentages should be read as approximate.
findings.method: sum(owners_mid) over percent_rank>=0.90 within genre, divided by genre total; bottom-bucket share = fraction with owners_low=0.
caveats: owners_mid, not measured sales; see scope_reminder.
This is reach/ownership concentration, not engagement or retention -- no playtime data exists in this dataset.
A game can carry multiple genre tags (fan-out is intentional here, not a join bug); a hit title's audience is counted once per genre it belongs to.

findings.claim: Catalogue-wide title supply has grown steadily and substantially every year (2015-2024), roughly 6.5x from 2,487 titles in 2015 to a 10-month partial count of 16,050 in 2024 -- this is a real, robust supply-side (developer enthusiasm) signal, unaffected by right-censoring since it is a simple count of releases.
findings.uncertainty: None for the count itself (a direct measurement); 2024's figure is a 10-month total (right-truncated at 2024-10-28, confirmed zero Nov/Dec rows) and understates the true full-year rate.
findings.method: COUNT(*) GROUP BY release_year, is_demo=false AND app_type='game' AND release_date IS NOT NULL.
caveats: 2024 is a partial year, not comparable 1:1 to prior full years.
20.4% of the catalogue has no release_date at all and is excluded from this cohort trend entirely -- if that missingness is not random across years, the true growth curve could differ.

findings.claim: Over the same 2015-2024 window, both mean owners_mid (199,630 to 32,096 by 2023) and median raw review_total (147 to 11 by 2023) fall sharply cohort-over-cohort. This decline is very largely a right-censoring artifact -- older cohorts have simply had more years to accumulate owners and reviews -- not clear evidence that per-title demand for new releases is falling; the true demand trend cannot be cleanly separated from time-since-release in this dataset.
findings.uncertainty: High -- this is explicitly a Simpson's-paradox / right-censoring risk named in the task brief. A partial correction (review_total annualized by days-since-release) reverses direction for the most recent cohorts (see F-minor below) but that correction is itself unstable for very young titles.
findings.method: AVG/MEDIAN owners_mid and review_total GROUP BY release_year.
caveats: Do not read the declining trend line as 'the market for new titles is shrinking' -- it is confounded with time-since-release by construction.
owners_mid proxy caveat as in scope_reminder.

findings.claim: Out-of-sample, a simple segment-expectation model (mean owners_mid by primary-genre x price-band, fit on a random 50% of titles and evaluated on the other, unseen half) has a real but weak positive relationship to actual holdout performance (Pearson r=0.114, Spearman-rank approx=0.297, n=57,522 holdout titles). Within that weak-but-real model, publisher-level residuals show existing Xbox-owned studios already outperforming their segment's expectation: Xbox Game Studios titles beat expectation by a median of 5.80x (n=32 holdout titles) and Bethesda Softworks by 6.23x (n=25) -- both comfortably above the >=5 holdout-title threshold set to exclude single-hit noise.
findings.segment: publisher, holdout half of catalogue only
findings.uncertainty: The overall model explains a small share of variance (r^2~0.01, rank corr ~0.30) -- genre and price band alone are weak predictors of reach; publisher-level residuals should be read as 'these publishers cleared a low, noisy bar consistently across >=5 titles the model never saw,' not as a precise multiplier.
findings.method: 50/50 hash(app_id) split; FIT-half mean owners_mid per (primary_genre, price_band) cell (n_fit>=30); primary_genre = each app's rarest global genre tag to avoid Indie/Action fan-out inflating title counts; residual = actual_owners_mid / FIT expectation, computed only on HOLDOUT rows the model never trained on.
caveats: owners_mid proxy caveat as in scope_reminder -- residual ratios inherit its coarseness.
Circularity check passed: publishers were not used to build the expectation model, and residuals are computed only on the held-out half never seen during fitting.

Lower-n publishers in the fuller table (n=5-9, e.g. Hi-Rez Studios 28.2x, Frozenbyte 7.26x) are directionally suggestive but noisier than the n>=25 entries highlighted here -- see sql_file for the full ranked list.
This is a Steam PC signal about Xbox's own existing first-party catalogue's PC performance, not a direct measurement of console/Game Pass performance.

findings.claim: Controlling for genre and price band via the same out-of-sample segment model, titles with a distinct publisher (developer != publisher) outperform self-published titles: mean residual ratio 1.610 vs 0.904, median 0.307 vs 0.250.
findings.uncertainty: is_self_published (developer==publisher string match) is an explicit proxy for 'has a distinct publisher backing it', not a real first/third-party field -- see DECISIONS.md. Reverse causality is plausible and not excludable with this data: a game that is already turning out well pre-launch may attract a publisher, rather than the publisher causing the outperformance.
findings.method: Same FIT/HOLDOUT segment-expectation model as F4, grouped by is_self_published on the holdout half only.
caveats: Observational association only, not causal -- cannot separate 'publisher backing helped' from 'publishers select projects that were already going to do well'.
owners_mid proxy caveat as in scope_reminder.

findings.claim: A large pool of well-reviewed, high-ownership 'proven hit' titles already exists per major genre across release vintages -- e.g. Action alone has 198 pre-2015, 217 from 2015-2019, 117 from 2020-2022 and 42 from 2023+ titles meeting a strict bar (owners_low>=1,000,000, review_total>=50, review_positive_ratio>=0.7). Sports, by contrast, has only 31 such titles across its entire history -- too thin to break out by vintage (n<30 in every bucket).
findings.metric: count of proven-hit titles by genre x vintage
findings.n: see value; every cell shown meets n>=30 except Sports, shown suppressed/flagged per its total
findings.uncertainty: This sizes a licensing candidate pool by catalogue inventory, not licensability, price, or exclusivity terms -- Xbox does not control which of these are actually available to license and at what cost.
findings.method: COUNT(DISTINCT app_id) meeting the hit bar, grouped by genre and a 4-bucket vintage split; cells with n<30 suppressed from the genre x vintage breakdown.
caveats: owners_low is a SteamSpy bucket floor (a coarse threshold, not a precise count) and review_positive_ratio depends on self-selected reviewers, which vary systematically by genre and audience size.

Sports' thinness on Steam is directly consistent with Stage 3's context finding that Steam's PC audience skews away from sports while Xbox's console audience skews toward it -- this dataset likely UNDERSTATES the real sports back-catalogue opportunity precisely because it is Steam/PC-only, not because sports games underperform.
A licensing decision needs console-side ownership data this dataset does not contain; treat this as a lower bound on genre coverage available on PC, not a console-transferable count.

findings.claim: Higher price bands associate with a larger estimated audience and far higher review volume up through $30-60, e.g. median review_total rises from 12 (under $5) to 456 ($30-60), before collapsing in the small $60+ band (n=353, median review_total 17) -- this is an observational, not causal, relationship: price is confounded with production budget/quality/marketing spend in this data and elasticity cannot be estimated causally here.
findings.segment: price band, paid titles with resolved USD price only
findings.uncertainty: Cannot separate price effect from quality/budget/marketing effect; treat as descriptive, not a demand curve.
findings.method: GROUP BY price band (paid titles, price_usd resolved via steamspy-primary/games.csv-fallback per DECISIONS.md), median/mean of owners_mid and review_total.
caveats: The $60+ band's collapse (n=353, low median reviews) is plausibly driven by a mix of older legacy-priced titles and a handful of anomalous listings rather than a real 'premium AAA underperforms' effect -- flagged as needing more investigation, not a board-ready claim on its own.
24.5% of nominally-paid titles (paid_price_unknown) are excluded entirely from every price-band statistic, not zeroed or imputed.

findings.claim: On Steam, shooter-family tags (Shooter 13,281 + FPS 7,789 + sub-genres) outnumber sports-family tags (Sports 4,983 + eSports 1,128) by roughly 3.5x -- a direct, catalogue-level confirmation of Stage 3's context claim that Steam's PC population skews toward shooters while Xbox's console population skews toward sports.
findings.segment: tag (from tags_long, not mutually exclusive per app)
findings.uncertainty: Tag counts measure how often creators/Steam's tagging system apply a label, not player population size directly, but at this scale (tens of thousands of tag rows) the shooter-vs-sports gap is not a small-sample artifact.
findings.method: COUNT(*) GROUP BY tag, filtered to shooter/sports/fps-family tag strings.
caveats: This is supply-side tag prevalence on PC/Steam, presented specifically as corroboration for a platform-population-mix caveat already established in Stage 3 -- it is not a new claim about player demand.

findings.claim: Discount behavior at the single Dec-2024 snapshot is fairly uniform across genres: 5-8.5% of paid titles were on sale that day, at a mean depth of 45-65% when discounted, with no genre a clear outlier.
findings.uncertainty: This is a single point-in-time observation, not discount frequency or a discount calendar -- the dataset has exactly one snapshot per app, so seasonal or promotional-cycle discount behavior cannot be measured at all.
findings.method: steamspy_stage.discount_pct_steamspy at snapshot, joined to genre.
caveats: Not decision-relevant on its own -- included for completeness, not as a headline finding.
Cannot distinguish 'genre discounts rarely' from 'the snapshot simply missed this genre's sale window'.

interesting_not_yet_defensible.note: A handful of developers show extreme out-of-sample residual ratios (e.g. Gas Powered Games 38.05x, Sometimes You 29.95x) but at n=3-4 holdout titles -- the minimum threshold used to exclude single-hit luck. Given the overall model's weak fit (r=0.114), these point estimates are highly noisy and should not be presented as board-grade evidence of repeat outperformance without a larger n or a longer observation window.

The 2023-2024 uptick in median reviews-per-year-since-release (7.9 in 2023, 15.5 in 2024, up from a 2018-2019 trough of ~4.1) looks like re-accelerating engagement velocity but is plausibly an artifact of review activity being front-loaded at launch: young titles' 'per-year' rate is annualized from only weeks of observed data, which mechanically inflates the rate versus mature cohorts where launch-week spikes are diluted by years of subsequent quiet. Needs a stricter minimum-age cutoff (e.g. >=180 days since release) before this can be treated as a real trend.
